title: Expelled
hook: England expels its Jews, the start of a long line of expulsions

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blood libels: a lie from Norwich that kept traveling. Your line was lies kill. Today a new week begins, in the same country, with an order from the king.

In the middle of London there is a street called Old Jewry. People walk down it to work every day, past banks and offices. The name is older than any of the buildings. It marks where a Jewish neighborhood once stood: homes, a synagogue, a place where children learned their letters. Then one summer a royal order went out across England, and by the autumn those homes were empty. Today, one word for what happened to them.
screen: `A LONDON STREET CALLED OLD JEWRY.` → `A ROYAL ORDER.` → `EMPTY HOMES BY AUTUMN.`

segments.voice: The king was Edward the First. His order told every Jew in England to leave the kingdom by the feast of All Saints; any who stayed after that would face death. They could take money and goods they could carry. Their houses, the debts owed to them and their synagogues passed to the crown. Some families crossed to France and other lands. Some, tradition says, did not survive the crossing. The order came at the end of a long squeeze. English Jews had been taxed again and again by the crown, restricted in the work they could do, and hit by the false stories we heard yesterday. By then the community was far poorer than it had been. Expelled is a hard word. It doesn't mean moved, or migrated. It means pushed out, with a deadline, by people with the power to enforce it. And England's order was not the last; other kingdoms and cities would issue their own over the following centuries. The Torah knows the experience from the inside. Its story keeps returning to leaving: Abraham told to go from his father's house, a people walking out of Egypt. And it turns that memory into a rule about others. In Exodus: "a stranger shalt thou not oppress; for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." A people that remembers being pushed out is asked to remember it every time someone else arrives at the door.
screen: `EDWARD THE FIRST'S ORDER.` · `LEAVE BY ALL SAINTS.` · `A LONG SQUEEZE BEFORE.` · then, large: `YE KNOW THE HEART OF A STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Picture your own front door and everything behind it you'd want to take, then imagine being told you have a few months, and only what you can carry. Let that settle, and widen the picture to the people, then and now, who have stood at that door for real. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words.
Expelled. Pushed out of a country by order, with a deadline: the fate of England's Jews under Edward the First, and of other communities after them. Today's word.
Your line: pushed out, with a deadline. Some street names still remember. That's day nine hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Jews remember past expulsions in study, in memorial prayers and on fast days such as Tisha B'Av, and some Jewish communities support refugees in memory of their own history.
